title: Class practical: experiment
stem: Answer with reference to the experiment you carried out as your class practical for learning and cognition.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe how you operationalized the independent and dependent variables in your experiment.
markscheme: IV identified
IV operationalized precisely, e.g. word list presented in silence vs with background music at a stated volume
DV identified
DV operationalized precisely, e.g. number of words correctly recalled in 2 minutes

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why you chose your sampling technique.
markscheme: technique identified, e.g. opportunity sampling of classmates
practical reason, e.g. quick, available, limited time
link to the target population of the study
limitation acknowledged, e.g. sample not representative so findings may not generalize

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain how two ethical considerations were applied in your experiment.
markscheme: first consideration identified, e.g. informed consent
how it was applied in this study, e.g. consent forms explaining procedure, parental consent for under-16s
why it mattered in this study
second consideration identified, e.g. right to withdraw / debriefing / confidentiality
how it was applied in this study
why it mattered in this study

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Discuss how bias may have affected the results of your experiment.
markscheme: a specific source of bias in the study identified, e.g. demand characteristics in a repeated measures design
how it could have affected the DV
a second source, e.g. researcher bias when scoring recall / sampling bias
how it could have affected the results
steps taken or that could be taken to reduce bias, e.g. counterbalancing, single-blind
judgement of the overall impact on conclusions

title: Unseen study: music and reading comprehension
stem: A researcher recruited 40 volunteers from a university psychology course through a social media post. Participants were allocated to one of two conditions by the order they arrived: the first 20 read a passage in silence, the next 20 read it while listening to songs with lyrics. All then answered 10 multiple-choice comprehension questions. The researcher, who expected music to impair comprehension, marked the answers and knew which condition each participant was in.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Evaluate this study with reference to measurement and causality.
markscheme: the mean is higher in silence (7.4 vs 6.1), suggesting a possible negative effect of music
the larger SD in the music condition shows more variable scores, so some music participants did well
allocation by arrival order is not random, so participant variables (e.g. early arrivers more motivated) may confound results, weakening causal claims
only 10 multiple-choice questions: a narrow operationalization of comprehension; possible ceiling effect
no inferential test reported, so the difference may not be significant
strength: the IV was manipulated with a control condition, so a causal claim is possible in principle
the type, volume and familiarity of the music were not controlled
reasoned judgement about how far the study supports a causal conclusion

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Discuss how bias may have affected this study.
markscheme: researcher bias: the researcher expected impairment and knew participants' conditions while marking
multiple-choice answers limit researcher bias in scoring, but expectations could affect instructions or interaction
sampling bias: self-selected psychology students may guess the aim and are not representative
demand characteristics: music participants may infer the hypothesis
improvement: double-blind marking and random allocation
improvement: a more diverse sample to increase generalizability
judgement of how far bias undermines the findings
